Orchot Tzadikim 14:11: The early sages would pray, "that our envy not be directed against others, nor the envy of others directed against us." Why would they pray about others more with regard to this trait than with regard to other traits? Because the matter is this: many people cause others to envy them and covet their fields; therefore they would pray about others, since they might be causing envy in others, and the Torah said (Leviticus 19:14), "and you shall not put a stumbling-block before the blind."
Orchot Tzadikim 14:12: Therefore it is a good trait in a person that he not wear overly fine and impressive garments — neither he, nor his wife, nor his children — and likewise regarding food and other matters, so that others not envy him. But whoever the Blessed Creator has favored with wealth and possessions should let others benefit from them, the rich and the poor, and should conduct himself gently with them, and do kindness with them. And we have already elaborated at length how good it is for a person to be beloved by his fellow creatures. And when he is beloved by everyone, they will not envy him or covet what is his. Rather, it is fitting for a person to rise to good qualities so that others envy him and desire to be like him. And whoever is careful not to envy — his body does not waste away, and worms do not dominate him, as it is written (Proverbs 14:30), "but envy is rottenness of the bones." Its meaning: whoever has envy, his bones rot (Shabbat 152b).
Orchot Tzadikim 14:13: Therefore let him keep far from envy and covetousness, and not covet anything that belongs to others. And let him not say: I shall covet something of my fellow's, and give him money for that item — for if he has no intention of selling his belongings, it is forbidden to press him, because he would be ashamed to turn him away empty-handed, and this is like coercion. And how much more so if the one who covets is an important man, whose face carries such weight that a request from him cannot be refused — it is forbidden to ask a gift of one's fellow unless he knows the other will give it with a willing soul.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:14: They told a parable: an envious man and a covetous man encountered a certain king. The king said to them: one of you shall ask something of me and it will be given to him, and to his fellow double. The envious man did not wish to ask first, for he would be envious if his fellow received double. And the covetous man desired both things. The covetous man pressed the envious man to ask; he asked to have one of his own eyes gouged out, so that his fellow would have both of his gouged out.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:15: How many evils depend on envy! The primordial serpent envied Adam, the first man, and brought death upon the world, and against it was decreed (Genesis 3:14), "on your belly shall you go, and dust shall you eat." And so see what happened to Cain, and to Korach, and to Balaam, and to Doeg, and to Achitophel, and to Gehazi, and to Adonijah, and to Absalom, and to Uzziah, who set their eyes on what was not theirs: not only was what they sought not given to them, but even what was already in their hands was taken from them. From all these let a person learn to keep away from envy and covetousness; for even what is in his own hand is not truly his, for tomorrow it may come and be gone — so what benefit is there in what is not truly his?
Orchot Tzadikim 14:16: There is great reward for a person who is careful about envy and covetousness. For with most transgressions, if a person is tempted to commit them yet feels shame, and restrains himself out of that shame — he restrains himself from robbery and theft because he fears it may become known, be revealed, and be publicized, bringing him shame and great loss. But envy and covetousness are matters of the heart: no one else can tell whether he covets or envies — behold, it is a matter entrusted to the heart alone, and of this it is said (Leviticus 25:17), "but you shall fear your God."
Orchot Tzadikim 14:17: Even though envy is a very bad trait, there is a place where it is very good, and it is the trait of the exalted: that he direct his envy toward the fear of Heaven, as the matter is said (Proverbs 23:17), "let not your heart envy sinners, but [continue] in the fear of the Lord all the day." And along this path our Sages of blessed memory said (Bava Batra 21a): the envy of scholars increases wisdom. For if a person sees another studying, envy takes hold in his heart and he says: this one studies all day, I too shall do the same! And likewise regarding all the commandments — each person envies his fellow, so as to take hold of his fellow's good deeds. If he sees a wicked man who has one good trait, he should envy him for that trait and do it as well. But whoever envies his fellow who is occupied with Torah and good deeds, not envying him in the sense of thinking "this one does so, I too shall do the same," but rather thinks in his heart and envies him because he has better qualities than himself, and is therefore more honored in the eyes of the world than himself, and schemes stratagems to nullify him and confound him away from his Torah study and his good deeds — this envy is a great evil, and he is a sinner and causes others to sin, a partner of Jeroboam ben Nevat.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:18: A person should always honor those who fear Heaven and occupy themselves with the commandments, and lend them a hand, and assist them with his person and his money. And then others will envy him and think: if we too do this, we too will be honored and helped. "And from [doing a commandment] not for its own sake, one comes to [do it] for its own sake."
Orchot Tzadikim 14:19: The Holy One, blessed be He, said: be envious for My sake! For were it not for envy, the world would not endure. For no person would plant a vineyard, no person would marry a wife, and no person would build a house; for all these matters come about because a person envies his fellow. If one builds a house, another too sets his mind to do the same. And likewise with a wife — each one envies his fellow. And since the endurance of the world depends on envy, one should direct all envy toward the sake of Heaven: if he builds a house, let him build in it a room to study Torah, and let his house be a meeting-place for the wise and a place to welcome guests (Avot 1:4-5), and to do kindness for people in it. And so our Sages of blessed memory said (Shocher Tov, ibid.): had Abraham our father not been envious, he would not have acquired heaven and earth. And when was he envious? When he said to Malchizedek: how did you come out of the ark? He said to him: through the charity we did there. He said to him: what charity could you have done in the ark — were there any poor people there? Were not only Noah and his sons there — with whom did you do charity? He said to him: with the beasts, the wild animals, and the birds. We did not sleep, but gave food and drink to this one and to that one. At that moment Abraham said: if these, were it not for the charity they did with the beasts, wild animals, and birds, would not have come out of the ark — and since they did charity, they came out — how much more so should I do charity with people, who are in the image of our God! At that moment, "and he planted an eshel" (Genesis 21:33) — an acronym for: eating, drinking, escort. Along this path let a person increase his envy.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:20: And likewise he should be envious [i.e. zealous] against sinners and the wicked, to fight against them and rebuke them, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 81b): whoever has relations with an Aramean woman — zealots may attack him.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:21: Moses was zealous against the Egyptian, as it is said (Exodus 2:12), "and he struck the Egyptian." And so we find with Elijah, as it is written (1 Kings 19:10), "I have been very zealous for the Lord, God of Hosts, for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant." And so it is said (Numbers 25:11), "in that he was zealous with My zeal among them." And the Blessed Lord gave him his reward for this, as it says (ibid. verse 12), "behold, I give to him My covenant of peace." And it is said (Deuteronomy 1:17), "you shall not be afraid of the face of any man." Whoever fears the Blessed Lord should give himself over for the sanctification of the Blessed Name, as it is said (Exodus 32:26), "whoever is for the Lord, come to me! And all the sons of Levi gathered to him." And it is said (Numbers 25:7), "and Pinchas the son of Elazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, and rose up from among the congregation, and took a spear in his hand."
Orchot Tzadikim 14:22: It is a duty upon every God-fearing person who is pure of heart to arouse zeal when he sees that the hand of the officers and the leaders is in the trespass. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Bereishit Rabbah 26:5): every breach that does not come from the great is not a breach, as it is said (Ezra 9:2), "and the hand of the officers and the leaders was first in this trespass."
Orchot Tzadikim 15:2: Diligence is a great trait for Torah and commandments, and also for the ordering of this world. And it is the trait of the righteous in the service of the Blessed Creator. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Pesachim 4a): the diligent perform commandments at the earliest opportunity.
Orchot Tzadikim 15:3: And behold, you see with Abraham our father, in the matter of the Binding [of Isaac], as it is said (Genesis 22:3), "and Abraham rose early in the morning..."; and even though it was hard for him to slaughter his only son, he performed the will of the exalted Creator with diligence, rising early in the morning. And whoever performs his deeds with diligence — this is great proof that he loves his Maker, like a servant who loves his master and hastens on his own to do his will. For diligence depends on a person's heart: when a person clears his heart of all other thoughts within it and takes hold of a single thought, he is diligent without doubt. So did Abraham do: he removed love of his son from his heart and took hold of the will of his Maker, setting aside love of his son for the sake of love of the Blessed Creator. And therefore he was diligent to rise early, because his mind was bound in love of the Blessed Creator with great longing; therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, swore to him to remember the Binding. For there is a person who does something very hard for him for the sake of one he loves, yet his heart still pricks him about doing it. But Abraham and Isaac both acted out of the desire of their own hearts, for the level of love was very great in their hearts; and both of them cleaved to the Blessed Lord in their knowledge, until they became united with Him in a great unity. For their entire intent was to publicize the unity of the Blessed Creator in the world, and to guide people toward love of Him. And at the time they performed the service of the exalted Lord and His commandments with love, the strength of their bodies was as though nullified, and their minds cleaved to love of the Blessed Creator, Maker of the world. Therefore both of them acted with diligence.
Orchot Tzadikim 15:4: And you must know that the trait of diligence is the beginning of all traits. For a person cannot be constantly at his books, since he must eat, sleep, and attend to his needs. Therefore diligence and care are needed, to return to his book and study. And let him not think: the day is still long, and the year is still long! For of this our Sages of blessed memory said (Avot 2:4): do not say, "when I am free I will study," lest you never become free. Also, a person should not say: "it is already evening; if I go to study, I will need to stand up at once to pray." For a single hour of study, even a single utterance, is better than anything in the world. Of this it is said (Proverbs 28:9), "whoever turns away his ear from hearing the Torah, even his prayer is an abomination." And it is written (Psalms 119:72), "the Torah of Your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver [pieces]." And it is said (ibid. 84:11), "for a day in Your courts is better than a thousand" — the Holy One, blessed be He, said: better to Me is one day that you occupy yourself with Torah, than a thousand burnt-offerings that your son Solomon is destined to offer before Me on the altar (Shabbat 30a).
Orchot Tzadikim 15:5: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair said: care leads to diligence, and diligence leads to cleanliness, and cleanliness leads to purity, and purity leads to abstinence, and abstinence leads to holiness, and holiness leads to humility, and humility leads to fear of sin, and fear of sin leads to piety, and piety leads to the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit leads to the resurrection of the dead, and the resurrection of the dead leads to [the coming of] Elijah the prophet, remembered for good (Yerushalmi Shekalim 3:3). Come and see how great is the power of diligence, that it leads to all these things! Therefore let a person be careful and diligent in all the commandments, and to run to his book to study, rising early and staying late.
Orchot Tzadikim 15:6: The trait of diligence is an adornment for all the commandments, and it perfects all of them. And now you should understand the matters in which people are habitually lazy.
Orchot Tzadikim 15:7: For instance, if you need to look up something in a book, strive to search for the matter you want, and be diligent to go and ask whoever knows the matter. If a poor man comes to your house to ask for bread, do not say, "I cannot go and bring the bread," but go with diligence to bring it. If you come to wash your hands, and you have only a little water, or dirty water, or the vessel is not so proper, such as having a crack in it, and you are hungry to eat — do not let your appetite lead you to be lax about the hand-washing; rather, be diligent to bring [proper] water and a vessel fit for hand-washing. And one must be especially diligent not to delay relieving oneself, even for a single moment, so as not to transgress "you shall not make yourselves disgusting" (Leviticus, cf. 20:25) (Makkot 16b). Also, one who delays relieving himself brings great illnesses upon himself (Bechorot 44b).
Orchot Tzadikim 15:8: And one must be careful and diligent to keep himself clean, so that his garments be clean and his body clean, washing the anus after relieving himself, since it is impossible to wipe properly without water. One must also be diligent, if he relieves himself at night near his bed, to rise and wash his hands, and go to a clean place to recite the blessing "asher yatzar." If he wishes to drink water, let him rise and wash his hands, and go to a clean place, and recite the blessing over the water both before and after. If he is in his bed and hears the sound of thunder or sees lightning, let him rise and wash his hands and recite the blessing. He must also rise from his bed and shake off drowsiness from his eyelids, and rise early to study Torah. And one must be diligent to separate himself from his bad thoughts, such as envy, hatred, and improper thoughts about women, for all these require very great diligence, to turn all his thoughts after the will of the Blessed Creator. If some grief comes upon him from the loss of his money, or the death of a loved one, or sufferings — he must be very diligent to strengthen, in his thoughts, love of the Rock of the world, to nullify the grief from his heart. And his heart should be pure, to justify God, blessed be He, in His judgments and rulings, accepting them out of love, and to cleave to Torah, prayer, and good deeds, and to strengthen himself with all his intent toward the exalted God.
Orchot Tzadikim 15:9: The general rule of the matter: a person should examine himself to see which transgression he is accustomed to, and hasten to make fences to be careful and guard himself from it. He should also examine himself to see in which commandment he is lax, and understand first what causes him to be lax in it. For instance, an idle person should first understand that his idleness comes from idle talk, and whoever devotes himself to idle talk becomes idle from Torah, prayer, and all good. Let him be diligent to remove himself from those who speak idle talk, and not associate with them — in this there is a remedy for his ailment. And so he should do for all bad traits: understand first the bad foundation, and demolish it, and remove from his eyes the darkness that darkens the light of his soul. And for all this diligence is needed to remove them, for if he is lazy about uprooting and rooting out these traits, they will form a root and branch in his heart that he will be unable to cut down. And let him be diligent to seek peace and pursue it, as it is said (Psalms 34:15), "seek peace and pursue it."
Orchot Tzadikim 15:10: And let him be diligent to seek knowledge of Torah and knowledge of the Blessed Creator, as it is written (Hosea 6:3), "let us pursue the knowledge of the Lord." And so our Sages said (Avot 4:13): exile yourself to a place of Torah. And let him be diligent to pursue righteousness, as it is written (Deuteronomy 16:20), "righteousness, righteousness shall you pursue"; and it is written (Isaiah 51:1), "listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the Lord." And he must be diligent to write down books he needs to study from. Or when he sees or hears some novel insight, let him be diligent to write it down, and not wait until it is forgotten from his heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 15:11: Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima said: be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and mighty as a lion, to do the will of your Father in Heaven (Avot 5:20). See how he warned him to make himself light and mighty for the commandments! And so David said (Psalms 119:60), "I hastened, and did not delay, to keep Your commandments." And so our Sages of blessed memory expounded: "and you shall guard the matzot (matzot)" (Exodus 12:17) — do not read "matzot" but "mitzvot": if a commandment comes into your hand, do not let it become leavened [i.e. delayed], but do it at once. And great lightness, diligence, and might are needed to fight against the wicked, to be strong-hearted like Moses our teacher, peace upon him, who said (Exodus 32:27), "let every man put his sword upon his thigh." And of Pinchas it is said (Numbers 25:7), "and Pinchas saw... and took a spear in his hand." Therefore be careful with yourself to be very diligent to separate from the company of the wicked, so as not to be in their counsel or their agreement. And above all one must be diligent to do teshuvah: let him hasten and not delay in the ways of teshuvah, and not remain wicked before the Blessed Omnipresent even for a single hour. See how the attendants of kings and officers are diligent in their errands and their service — how much more so should one be careful and diligent to perform the service of the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
Orchot Tzadikim 15:12: Even though diligence is very good, one must be careful not to rush his service excessively. For one who rides swiftly is very close to stumbling, and likewise one who runs swiftly falls. And it is not possible to properly complete a deed in haste, but matters are properly completed with deliberation. And so our Sages said (Avot 1:1): be deliberate in judgment. And true diligence is this: that one's heart be awake, and his thoughts alert, and his limbs be light for his work; but he should not rush in any matter. And all these matters require great wisdom, to know when to hasten and when to delay. And even though the trait of diligence is very good, one should not be diligent to pursue his desires, and to toil after his pleasures, and to pursue his bad deeds. For just as diligence in Torah matters brings a person to the highest level, so diligence in transgressions brings a person down to the depths of Sheol.
Orchot Tzadikim 15:13: And just as diligence is needed for Torah, so diligence is needed for the affairs of this world: that he be diligent in his work. And there is great success for whoever does his affairs with diligence. Therefore, O son of man, be diligent for both worlds, and do your work — which is the needs of this world — with diligence, so that you may quickly become free for the work of Heaven.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:2: Laziness is a very bad trait. Whoever is dominated by this trait has his affairs greatly corrupted in this world and in the World to Come. Of him King Solomon, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 24:30-31), "I passed by the field of a lazy man, and by the vineyard of a man lacking sense; and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns, nettles had covered its surface, and its stone wall was broken down." He compared the wisdom of the lazy man to the field of a lazy man: for just as the field of a lazy man is not only lacking in produce, because he does not work it as he should, but even grows bad things, such as nettles and thorns that damage the crop — even if he had troubled himself over his field until produce grew, he would lose everything because of his laziness. For his stone wall is broken down, and being lazy he does not repair the wall, and through this animals and thieves enter and take everything. And it says, "its stone wall was broken down" — even though a stone wall is very strong, nonetheless it becomes broken down because of his laziness, for he did not repair its deficiency before it collapsed entirely.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:3: So it is with the matter of the lazy man regarding Torah and commandments: for the lazy love rest, and because of this the commandments are hard for them, and the study of Torah is heavy upon their souls, and they flee from the study halls to their place of rest. And when they sit in the synagogue, they sleep, as the matter is said (Proverbs 19:15), "laziness casts one into a deep sleep"; for laziness brings sleep upon a person's nature. And King Solomon, peace upon him, already warned (ibid. 6:10), "a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest."
Orchot Tzadikim 16:4: It is not enough for the lazy man that he does not attain knowledge of Torah, since he does not occupy himself with Torah properly; but because of his laziness he also raises up mistaken reasonings in his heart. For the lazy man permits things to himself and says: "rest is good for the body, so that it grow strong, for when a person is strong he can do more than the weak." And he inclines his ears to idle talk, saying that this will open his heart. It follows that laziness causes him to search for reasonings, to say that he performs a commandment by becoming idle from study. Even though this reasoning is true — that it is good to rest in order to grow strong, or to hear words of jest to open the heart — this applies specifically to a person who is diligent and occupies himself with Torah properly. For a person's strength is not like the strength of stones, nor are his bones like copper, to toil constantly, and sometimes he needs to rest in order to grow strong. But the lazy man straightens out this reasoning for himself, and is drawn after it until he becomes idle from everything. And always, in every commandment that involves effort, he will make a reasoning, out of his laziness, to become idle from the commandment. In sum: the lazy man bends all his reasonings toward the side of laziness.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:5: The lazy man is soft-hearted, and does not exile himself to a place of Torah. And of him King Solomon said seven things (Devarim Rabbah 8:6). How so? They say to the lazy man: "your teacher is in the city, go and learn Torah from him!" And he answers them: "I am afraid of the lion on the road," as it is said (Proverbs 26:13), "the lazy man says, there is a lion in the road." They say to him: "your teacher is within the province, get up and go to him!" And he answers them: "I am afraid a lion may come into the streets," as it is said (ibid.), "a lion is in the streets." They say to him: "behold, he lives near your house!" And he answers them: "the lion is outside," as it is said (ibid. 22:13), "the lazy man says, there is a lion outside, I shall be murdered in the streets." They say to him: "behold, he is inside the house." And he answers them: "if I go and find the door locked, I will have to turn back." They say to him: "it is open" — still the lazy man will not get up, as it is said (ibid. 26:14), "as the door turns on its hinges, so does the lazy man on his bed." And in the end, not knowing what else to answer, he tells them: "whether the door is open or locked, I wish to sleep a little more." As it is said (ibid. 6:9), "how long will you sleep, O lazy man? When will you arise from your sleep?" He gets up from his bed, and they set food before him — and he is too lazy to put it into his mouth, as it is said (ibid. 26:15), "the lazy man buries his hand in the dish; he is too weary to bring it back to his mouth."
Orchot Tzadikim 16:6: And what is the seventh thing? As it is said (ibid. 20:4), "the lazy man will not plow because of the cold." Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai said: this refers to one who did not study Torah in his youth, and wishes to study in his old age, and cannot. And this is [the continuation] (ibid.), "he shall beg at harvest time, and have nothing."
Orchot Tzadikim 16:7: Until here Solomon disparaged the lazy man. And Moses our teacher, peace upon him, said something greater than all of this, as it is said (Deuteronomy 30:14), "for the thing is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it." Its meaning: only bring the words out of your mouth. And whoever is too lazy for even this, not bringing words out of his mouth — there is no laziness greater than this.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:8: See how far the lazy man is from good traits, and how utterly unfit he is for any errand — like vinegar, which is unfit for the teeth, as it is said (Proverbs 10:26), "as vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the lazy man to those who send him." And it is said (ibid. 26:16), "the lazy man is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can give a sensible answer." The meaning of this verse is this: a king who has many runners and messengers, and they all performed the king's errand, and also gave an answer to the king when they returned from their errand. But one of the king's servants was a lazy man, and he pretended, saying "I am sick," and rested and ate from the king's table. And when he saw his fellows coming weary from the toil of the road, he then considered himself wiser than all his fellows in his own eyes. But this is folly on his part, as it is written (ibid. 22:29), "do you see a man diligent in his work? He shall stand before kings." And here too the king will pay reward to the clever ones, who gave him a sensible answer; but he will not concern himself with the lazy man at all.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:9: In sum: the lazy man is worth nothing, neither in this world nor in the World to Come, for his hands refuse to do good. And the wise man said: the laziest of people is one who was too lazy to acquire wise and God-fearing friends. And there is one lazier still: one who had all these already in hand and lost them.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:10: The Holy One, blessed be He, created a weak creature, which stores up its food and toils for its sustenance, in order to teach wisdom through it to the lazy man, as it is written (Proverbs 6:6), "go to the ant, you lazy one; consider her ways, and be wise." Therefore let him be ashamed upon seeing the weak ant, diligent in its affairs, and let him learn from it to take hold, as it does, of the trait of diligence, and to come out from under the hand of laziness, and to save his soul from the pit.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:11: And there is a laziness that is very good, such as one who sits and is lazy to do bad things and to pursue desires. It is told of a man whom the king wished to send to a place of danger, and he did not wish to go, and the king reviled him. He then said to the king: better that you revile me while I am alive, than that you pray for me while I am dead.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:12: And of this matter our Sages said (Pesachim 50b): there is a diligent man who gains, and a diligent man who loses; there is a lazy man who gains, and a lazy man who loses. Diligent and gains — one who does his work all week and does not do it on the eve of the Sabbath. Diligent and loses — one who does work all week, and also does it on the eve of the Sabbath. Lazy and gains — one who does no work all week, and does none on the eve of the Sabbath. Lazy and loses — one who does no work all week, but does work on the eve of the Sabbath. See how our Sages recognized that there is a diligence that is good and a diligence that is bad, and likewise with laziness.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:13: Therefore resolve to do good with all your limbs and all your thoughts, and choose, for each and every limb, a measure of lightness and a measure of heaviness, all for the sake of Heaven: be light to sit with friends who join together for Torah and commandments, and be heavy [i.e. reluctant] to sit with scoffers and doers of evil. Be light in your own eyes to look into religious law and matters of the commandments, and be heavy in your eyes to look at vain deeds, and to gaze at a married woman or at idolatry. Be light in your ears to hear ethical teachings, rebukes, and matters of Torah law, and be heavy in your ears to hear vulgar speech and idle talk. Be light in your nostrils to be angry at the wicked, and be heavy in your nostrils to be angry at the righteous. Be heavy in your mouth and your tongue regarding quarrels, falsehoods, mockery, and slander, and be light in your mouth with words of Torah, rebukes, and commanding the good.
Orchot Tzadikim 16:14: Be heavy in your hand to raise a hand against your fellow, and be light in your hand to give charity, and to do your work faithfully. Be heavy in your feet to walk in the ways of the wicked, to go to feasts and to outings, and be light in your feet to run to synagogues and study halls, and to visit the sick, and to accompany [the dead or a bride], and to all the commandments. Be heavy in your heart to think bad thoughts, and be heavy regarding envy and hatred, and be light in your heart to think thoughts of Torah, and to attain the virtues of love of the Blessed Lord and pure fear of Him. And by this you will be light and diligent in your heart to cleave to the supernal light.
